**Proposition.** For a system $S$ with state space $\Omega$ and symmetry group $G$ acting on $\Omega$, the observable diversity $D(S)$ satisfies $D(S) \geq |\Omega/G| - |\text{Stab}(G)|$, where $\Omega/G$ is the orbit space and $\text{Stab}(G)$ is the set of stabilizer subgroups, with equality when all symmetries are manifest and strict inequality when symmetries are spontaneously broken.

**Proof.** Let $\Omega$ be a smooth manifold of finite dimension $n$ and let $G$ be a Lie group acting smoothly and properly on $\Omega$, with the action being free outside a measure-zero set. We assume the physical observables form a $C^*$-algebra $\mathcal{A}$ on which $G$ acts by automorphisms, and that the observable diversity $D(S)$ counts the cardinality of distinguishable macroscopic states. Further, let $E: \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be a $G$-invariant energy functional that is bounded below, with vacuum manifold $V \subset \Omega$ consisting of all minimum energy states.

By definition, the orbit space $\Omega/G$ parametrizes equivalence classes of states under symmetry transformations. When all symmetries are manifest, $G$-invariant observables cannot distinguish between states within the same orbit, establishing a bijection between observable states and orbits in $\Omega/G$. Thus, in the symmetric phase, $D(S) = |\Omega/G|$.

Now consider spontaneous symmetry breaking. Since the energy functional is $G$-invariant, we have $G \cdot v \subset V$ for any $v \in V$, implying that the vacuum manifold decomposes as $V = \bigcup_i G \cdot v_i$ where the $v_i$ are representatives of distinct orbits. 

For spontaneous symmetry breaking to occur, there must exist a vacuum state $v_0 \in V$ whose stabilizer $H = \text{Stab}_G(v_0)$ is a proper subgroup of $G$. By the Orbit-Stabilizer Theorem, the orbit $G \cdot v_0 \cong G/H$ has dimension $\dim(G) - \dim(H) > 0$, since $H \subsetneq G$ implies $\dim(H) < \dim(G)$.

When the system physically selects the vacuum state $v_0$, the original $G$-symmetry is broken to the residual $H$-symmetry. Crucially, the $|G/H|$ distinct points in the orbit $G \cdot v_0$, which were previously related by symmetry, now become physically distinguishable vacuum states. This multiplies the observable diversity by a factor of $|G/H|$ for each symmetry-broken sector.

More generally, if the state space decomposes into symmetry sectors $\Omega_i$ with residual symmetries $H_i$ after breaking, the total observable diversity becomes
$$D(S) = \sum_i |G/H_i| \cdot |\Omega_i/H_i|$$

[Note: A fully rigorous counting of distinguishable states requires careful measure-theoretic treatment of the orbit spaces, which we have not provided here.]

Since $|G/H_i| \geq 1$ with equality if and only if $H_i = G$ (no symmetry breaking), we obtain $D(S) \geq |\Omega/G|$. Equality holds precisely when all $H_i = G$, meaning no symmetry is broken. When spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs in any sector, we have $H_i \subsetneq G$ for some $i$, yielding $|G/H_i| > 1$ and thus $D(S) > |\Omega/G|$.

This completes the proof. □
